Papal Infallibility
PAY-pul in-fal-ih-BIL-ih-tee
noun phrase (a Roman dogma)
From “papal” (of the pope) and “infallibility” (incapacity of error); the Roman dogma, defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870, that the pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra.

📖 Biblical Definition

Papal infallibility is the Roman Catholic dogma, defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870, that the pope, when he speaks ex cathedra—that is, when as supreme pastor he defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole church—is preserved from error by divine assistance and his definitions are irreformable of themselves. The dictionary rejects this dogma as contrary to Scripture and as a corruption of the unique authority that belongs to the Word of God alone. Scripture knows but one infallible rule of faith, the inspired Word, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; it nowhere grants an unerring teaching office to any man or succession of men. Peter himself, whom Rome claims as the first pope, was openly rebuked by Paul to his face at Antioch because he was to be blamed—a plain proof that the apostle was not impeccable or unerring in his conduct, still less his supposed successors. The Lord forbade His disciples the very titles and lordship the papacy assumed: “call no man your father upon the earth.” And the noble Bereans were commended for searching the Scriptures daily to test even apostolic preaching, the very opposite of a blind submission to an infallible chair. The dictionary holds that the conscience is bound by Scripture alone (sola Scriptura); councils and bishops may err and have erred; and the claim of an infallible pope, far from securing the truth, has been the instrument of binding the church to errors—indulgences, Marian dogmas, the denial of justification by faith alone—that the Reformation called the church away from on the authority of the Word of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Roman dogma (Vatican I, 1870) that the pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra; rejected as contrary to Scripture, which knows one infallible rule (the Word) and one Mediator, and records Peter himself rebuked by Paul.

PAPAL INFALLIBILITY, noun phrase. The Roman dogma that the pope cannot err when defining doctrine ex cathedra.

Defined at the First Vatican Council in 1870.

Rejected as contrary to sola Scriptura: one infallible rule, the inspired Word.

Peter, claimed as first pope, was openly rebuked by Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11).

The Lord forbade the very lordship and titles the papacy assumed (Matthew 23:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Ga 2:11 — "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

1 Ti 2:5 — "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;"

Mt 23:9 — "And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven."

Ac 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Papal infallibility is itself the corruption: it usurps for a man the unerring authority Scripture grants to the Word of God alone, and has been used to bind the church to grave error.

expand to see more

Papal infallibility is not a doctrine the dictionary must guard against drift; it is itself the corruption to be named. Rome claims for the pope, speaking ex cathedra, an immunity from error that Scripture grants to no man. But the Word of God is the only infallible rule of faith, and Christ the only Mediator; the apostles themselves directed the churches to test all teaching by the Scriptures, and Peter—the supposed first pope—was withstood to the face by Paul and blamed. An office that can be rebuked is not an office that cannot err. The dogma exalts a man into the place that belongs to the Word.

The practical fruit of the dogma exposes its falsehood. Far from preserving the church in truth, the claim of infallible papal authority has been the very instrument by which grave errors were imposed and made irreformable—the sale of indulgences, the dogmas of the Immaculate Conception and the bodily Assumption of Mary, the anathemas of Trent against justification by faith alone. The Reformation did not invent a new authority but recalled the church to the old and only one: the Scriptures, which are able to make wise unto salvation, and to which pope, council, and conscience alike must bow. Sola Scriptura is the dictionary's answer to the infallible chair.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin papa (pope, father) and in- + fallere (not to deceive or err); the dogma rests on the claim of an unerring teaching office, denied by Scripture's sole rule.

expand to see more

Papa, Latin, “father,” the title of the Bishop of Rome.

Ex cathedra, Latin, “from the chair,” the supposed condition of infallible definition.

Infallibilis, Latin, “incapable of error,” from fallere, to deceive.

Defined dogmatically at the First Vatican Council, 1870.

Set against sola Scriptura, the sole infallible rule of faith.

Usage

"The teacher answered papal infallibility by showing Peter himself rebuked by Paul at Antioch."

"He held that the conscience is bound by Scripture alone, not by an infallible chair."

"She searched the Scriptures like the noble Bereans, testing all teaching by the Word."
